THOUGHT: The CT and MRI show a biphasic mass in the right cerebellopontine angle: a medial component with negative Hounsfield units on CT and T1 hyperintensity that suppresses on fat-saturated T1 — consistent with true fat (intracranial lipoma or fat-containing cyst). The lateral component is isointense on T1, shows nodular enhancement on postcontrast fat‑sat T1, extends through a widened porus acusticus into the internal auditory canal without bone destruction — classic imaging behavior for a vestibular (acoustic) schwannoma. The combination of a nonenhancing fatty lesion medially and an enhancing IAC-extending lesion laterally most straightforwardly represents two coexisting lesions (a CPA lipoma adjacent to a vestibular schwannoma) — a documented but uncommon “collision” appearance. Other possibilities include a single mixed lesion that contains fat and solid enhancing elements (mature teratoma, dermoid with solid/ inflammatory nodule) or fat-containing/“lipomatous” variants of other CPA tumors (rare lipomatous meningioma). Epidermoid is unlikely because of true fat signal and suppression; liposarcoma or metastasis would be very rare.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Collision lesion: Vestibular schwannoma (enhancing lateral/IAC component) with adjacent CPA intracranial lipoma (medial fat component) — most likely
2) Mature teratoma of the CPA (fat + enhancing soft‑tissue elements) — less likely but can show mixed fat and solid enhancing tissue
3) Dermoid cyst with associated enhancing nodular component or inflammatory change — possible but CPA dermoids are uncommon and often midline
4) Lipomatous (fat‑containing) meningioma in the CPA — rare; would usually be dural‑based
5) Primary intracranial liposarcoma or other fat‑containing metastatic/primary malignant tumor of the CPA — very rare but considered for mixed fat + enhancing soft tissue
ground_truth: Mature cystic teratoma of the cerebellopontine angle (CPA)
